t.batu tabal train station@-0.5,100.5:
High in the mountains of West Sumatra, a railway line built by the Dutch in the late nineteenth century snakes between volcanoes, lakes and rice terraces. It was laid to carry coal from the mines of Sawahlunto down to the port of Padang, and the whole system, mines, company town and railway, forms the Ombilin Coal Mining Heritage of Sawahlunto, listed by UNESCO in 2019. Batu Tabal is one of the small stations along the route, near the shores of Lake Singkarak, where the line runs right along the water's edge.

The railway was a remarkable feat of engineering, with steep sections that required a rack and pinion system to haul trains up through the Anai valley gorge. Much of it is now disused, though occasional tourist trains run on parts of the line. Rusting tracks, small station buildings and old bridges are scattered across the landscape, slowly being reclaimed by tropical vegetation.

This is the land of the Minangkabau, one of the world's largest matrilineal societies, where property and family names pass through the female line. Their traditional houses, rumah gadang, have dramatic curved roofs rising to sharp points like buffalo horns, and you will see them in villages around the lake. The region is also the birthplace of rendang, the slow-cooked spicy beef that is often listed among the best dishes in the world, and Padang restaurants, where many small dishes are laid out on the table at once, are found across Indonesia.

Riding here is spectacular and demanding. Roads around Lake Singkarak and between the towns of Padang Panjang, Solok and Bukittinggi wind through hills, terraces and forests, with views of volcanoes such as Marapi. Traffic can be heavy, with trucks, buses and countless scooters, and driving is on the left. The road down to Padang through the Anai valley passes a waterfall right beside the road. Rain is frequent and heavy, especially in the afternoons, and roads can flood or suffer landslides.

Fuel is available in towns and larger villages, often at small roadside stalls selling petrol in bottles as well as at proper stations. Solok and Padang Panjang are the nearest large towns. Try fresh fish from the lake, called bilih, fried crisp, or a full Padang meal at a roadside restaurant overlooking the water.
t.site 12@19.5,103.4:
Imagine hundreds of huge stone jars scattered across a high plateau, some taller than a person, some lying on their sides, some cracked open by time or by bombs. That is the Plain of Jars in Xieng Khouang province, Laos, and nobody knows for certain who made them or why. Archaeologists believe they are about two thousand years old or more, and that they were connected with burial practices; local legend says they were made to brew rice wine to celebrate a great victory. Since 2019 a selection of the jar sites has been listed by UNESCO as the Megalithic Jar Sites in Xiengkhuang. Site 12 is one of the smaller groups, out in the countryside some twenty-five kilometres from the provincial capital, Phonsavan.

The landscape is beautiful, rolling hills of grass and pine, rice paddies and villages of wooden houses, at an altitude that makes the air noticeably cooler than in the lowlands. But it carries a terrible legacy. During the Vietnam War, Laos became the most heavily bombed country per person in history, and this province was hit especially hard. Unexploded ordnance still litters the land, and clearance teams continue to work. At the jar sites, cleared paths are marked; stay on them, without exception.

Phonsavan has a visitor centre run by a mine clearance organisation that explains the history and the ongoing work, and it is well worth a visit.

The riding to get here is an adventure. Route 7 runs from the junction at Phou Khoun, on the road between Vientiane and Luang Prabang, east across the mountains to Phonsavan, with endless bends, steep climbs and spectacular views. Surfaces vary from good asphalt to broken, potholed sections, and you will share the road with trucks, buses, scooters, buffalo and children. The smaller roads to the outlying jar sites are often dirt, muddy in the rainy season and dusty in the dry.

Phonsavan has fuel, guesthouses, restaurants and motorbike rentals. Outside town, fuel is scarce, sold from bottles at roadside stalls in some villages. The best time to visit is the dry season, from November to April; nights can be cold on the plateau in December and January. The rainy season, from May to October, makes the dirt roads very difficult.
t.site 28@19.6,102.9:
The Plain of Jars is one of the great archaeological puzzles of Southeast Asia: hundreds of carved stone jars, some taller than a person and weighing several tonnes, scattered across hillsides and meadows of the Xieng Khouang plateau in northern Laos. Site 28 is one of the many smaller groups, far less visited than the famous Site 1 near Phonsavan, and the coordinates place it out in the countryside to the west of town, among rolling grassland, scattered pines and farmed valleys.

Archaeologists have connected the jars with Iron Age funerary practices dating back somewhere around two thousand years or more. Human remains, beads and tools have been found near them, and the leading theory is that bodies were placed in the jars to decompose before the bones were buried. Who carved them, and exactly why in this place, is still uncertain. UNESCO listed the jar sites in 2019, recognising both their mystery and their fragility.

The other history of this plateau is harder and more recent. Between 1964 and 1973, during the Vietnam War and the so-called Secret War in Laos, this region was bombed relentlessly by the United States, and Laos remains, per capita, one of the most heavily bombed countries in history. Unexploded cluster bombs still lie in the fields. The jar sites open to visitors have been cleared by organisations such as the Mines Advisory Group, and marked paths show where it is safe to walk. Stay on them without exception. Bomb craters are visible all around, and you may see shell casings used as house posts and planters in the villages.

The riding is rewarding and rough. From Phonsavan, roads fan out across the plateau, mostly paved on the main routes but quickly turning to red dirt and gravel on the way to outlying sites, which become slick and rutted in the rainy season from about May to October. The altitude, around a thousand metres, makes the air pleasant compared to the lowlands, and mornings in the dry season can be truly chilly.

Muang Phônsavan, some thirty-five kilometres away, is the only real base, with fuel stations, guesthouses, restaurants and the information centre of the Mines Advisory Group, which explains the bombing and the clearance work and is well worth an hour. Fill up there, carry water, and ask locally about the state of the tracks before setting out.
t.site 25@19.6,103.1:
Local legend has a cheerful explanation for the stone jars of Xieng Khouang. It tells of Khun Cheung, a legendary king who won a great victory and ordered the jars carved so that his people could brew lao-lao, the rice spirit, in huge quantities for the celebration. Archaeology prefers a funerary purpose, but the story says a lot about how people here like to see their past, and it is a good one to share over a glass of the real thing in the evening.

Site 25 is one of the scattered jar groups that make up the Plain of Jars, listed by UNESCO in 2019, and it lies some twenty kilometres from Phonsavan among the grassy hills of the plateau. The jars were cut from sandstone and other rock, some with stone lids lying nearby, a few decorated with faint carvings. They stand at odd angles in the grass, tilted by time, some cracked by tree roots, some by bombs. Many sites also have stone discs that may have covered burials. Standing among them in the evening light, with cattle grazing in the next field, is a strange and gentle experience.

The plateau has a character of its own. At around a thousand metres, it is high enough to be cool, and the landscape is more open than most of Laos, with grassy slopes, pine groves, rice paddies in the valleys and limestone hills on the horizon. Many villages are Hmong, and the market in Phonsavan is the place to see their textiles and the produce of the hills. The bombing of the 1960s and early 1970s has left its mark on all of it, and unexploded ordnance is still a danger: walk only within the cleared and marked areas.

On a bike, the approach to a site like this is part of the charm. Expect a paved main road out of Phonsavan, then a side track of red earth, rutted and dusty in the dry season and sticky with mud in the wet, with chickens, children and water buffalo for company. A dual-sport bike is the right tool. Ride slowly through the villages; this is not a place to be in a hurry.

Fuel, guesthouses and food are in Muang Phônsavan, along with the information centre of the clearance organisations. Fill up there, carry water and a little food, and bring a warm layer for the evenings, which can be surprisingly cold between November and February.
t.salak power plant and ranith water pumpi:
Coal built this corner of West Sumatra, and the buildings at Salak and the Ranith pumping station are part of the machinery that moved it. The Dutch colonial government developed the Ombilin coalfield after a geologist found rich seams near Sawahlunto in the nineteenth century, and the whole system of mine, railway, power plant and port was later recognised by UNESCO as the Ombilin Coal Mining Heritage of Sawahlunto. A power station gave the mines electricity, and a pumping station supplied water, because a steam age needs both.

The surrounding landscape is nothing like the industrial image. The highlands of Minangkabau country are steep, green and wet, with terraced rice fields, palm and clove trees, and villages of curved-roof houses that look like buffalo horns. Solok, the nearest big town, is known for its rice, and not far away lies Lake Singkarak, a large, cool lake in a tectonic basin that is one of the pleasures of the region. The Minangkabau are the world's largest matrilineal society, with property passing through the women of a family, which gives the culture a particular character.

For riding, this is a rewarding but demanding part of Indonesia. The roads that climb from Padang toward Solok and Sawahlunto wind through forest and ravines, with tight bends, steep gradients and trucks grinding uphill in clouds of exhaust. Surfaces are often patched and uneven, rain arrives in torrential afternoon bursts, and landslides can close sections after heavy weather. Mornings are the best time, when the air is clear and the mountains show. The dry season, roughly June to September, is easier, though rain is never far off near the equator.

Solok, about twenty kilometres away, is the place for fuel, a meal and a rest. Minangkabau cuisine is famous across Indonesia, and Padang-style restaurants serve rendang, slow-cooked beef in coconut and spices, alongside curries, chillies and rice, with dishes brought to your table in a crowd of small plates that you pay for by what you eat. Fill up before the hills, carry water, and wear a rain jacket, because on this side of the island the sky changes its mind quickly.
t.site 23@19.5,103.7:
Nobody agrees on who made the stone jars of Xieng Khouang, or exactly why. They are scattered over a high plateau in northern Laos, thousands of stone vessels, some of them taller than a person, carved from rock and set in groups on grassy hillsides, dating from perhaps two thousand years ago. The usual explanation is that they were used in funerary rites by an Iron Age culture, and archaeologists have found human remains and burial goods near them, which supports that, but folklore says they were brewing vessels for a giant king's victory feast. The UNESCO listing of 2019 covers a number of different sites, and Site 23 is one of the smaller, less visited ones, so I can tell you about the region better than I can describe the exact spot.

The plateau is around a thousand metres high, with cool air, red earth, pine trees, and rolling pasture where buffalo graze. The main town is Phonsavan, with fuel, markets and basic guesthouses, and it is the sensible base. Remember that this area was among the most heavily bombed in history during the war of the 1960s and 1970s, and unexploded ordnance is still in the ground. Stay on marked paths, usually painted with red and white stones, and never wander off into a field, however empty it looks.

The ride up to the plateau from the lowlands is the real event. Roads climb through steep forested hills, with hairpins, landslides in the wet season, rough patches of broken asphalt and slow trucks, and the surface can change from smooth to gravel without warning. Mist hangs on the ridges in the morning, and the air smells of wood smoke. There are few fuel stations outside the towns, so fill the tank before the climb and carry water.

The best months are November to February, when the air is cool and dry, and the nights are cold enough to want a jacket. From March the fields are burned and a haze hangs in the air, and from June to September the rains make tracks slippery. Ask in Phonsavan about road conditions, take a local guide to the lesser sites, and drink a cup of strong Lao coffee in the morning, because the mountains deserve a clear head.
t.six gun battery@13.5,-16.6:
The Gambia is a long, narrow country that follows its river, and Banjul sits at the mouth where the river meets the Atlantic, on a low, sandy island that feels like a sandbar with ambitions. The city was founded by the British in 1816 as Bathurst, a base to suppress the slave trade, and the Six-Gun Battery is one of the military remains from that era. It forms part of the UNESCO site called Kunta Kinteh Island and Related Sites, which also includes Fort Bullen on the opposite bank at Barra, and together they tell the story of the Gambia river as a route of the Atlantic slave trade and of the later effort to end it.

The battery itself is modest, with old cannon pointing out toward the water, but the setting makes it powerful. The two forts faced each other across the mouth of the river, and between them the river is wide, brown and strong. The story is bound up with the names of the river, among them Kunta Kinteh Island, upstream, which Alex Haley made famous in his novel Roots. The wind off the sea is steady and salty, and the light in the late afternoon is soft and golden.

The riding is not what you would call challenging. The Gambia is flat, hot and small, with a coast road of surprisingly good tarmac, red laterite side roads, and plenty of police checkpoints, where a friendly greeting is usually enough. Heat is intense from March to May, and the rainy season from July to October brings heavy storms and flooded tracks. The best months are November to February, when the days are warm and dry. Banjul itself is crowded and chaotic, with markets, mopeds and goats, and driving requires patience.

To cross to Barra, you take the ferry, which is a slow and sometimes unreliable experience, with long queues and an unpredictable schedule, so bring patience, snacks and water. Banjul and the nearby towns, such as Serrekunda, have fuel and shops, and Barra has the basics. Food is excellent, especially grilled fish, domoda, a peanut stew, and fresh bread, and a cold Julbrew beer or fresh ginger drink makes a good finish.
t.kerbatch@13.8,-15.1:
Stones that nobody can explain are scattered across the Gambian countryside, and Kerbatch has some of them. The stone circles of Senegambia, a World Heritage site since 2006, are a group of more than a thousand megaliths in about thirty circles, set in a band of land along the river Gambia and into Senegal. Each stone is a carved pillar of laterite, a rust-red, iron-rich rock that is cut from the ground when it is soft and hardens in the sun, and they stand in rings of ten to twenty, sometimes with a larger stone set to one side. They were raised between roughly the third century BC and the sixteenth century AD, and they mark burials, some of which have been excavated and found to hold skeletons and grave goods.

Nobody knows who built them. The local people say the circles were always there, and archaeologists link them to ancient communities of farmers and ironworkers who lived along the river, but the beliefs behind them are lost. Kerbatch is a smaller group than the better-known sites at Wassu, which has a small museum and eleven circles, and at Sine Ngayene in Senegal, which has the largest number of stones, but there is something affecting about standing in a quiet field among a ring of old pillars with a view of acacia and baobab trees.

The roads here are a typical West African mix. The main highway along the south bank of the Gambia is a long, straight road with a patched surface, and the pace is determined by potholes, goats, donkey carts, minibuses and the occasional police checkpoint, which is normally polite and brief. The dry season, from November to May, is the only sensible time to ride, since the rains from June to October flood the tracks and turn the red laterite into mud. In the middle of the day the heat is intense, so start early, carry plenty of water and wear a light, breathable layer.

Karantaba, with about seventeen hundred people, and Kass Wollof are small villages, so fill up with fuel in a larger town such as Soma or Farafenni before you leave. The village women sell groundnuts, mangoes and sweet tea, and the hospitality is warm, with greetings that can go on for some time.
t.eagle plains@66.4,-136.7:
Eagle Plains is a small dot of civilisation on the Dempster Highway, a gravel road that runs from near Dawson City, in the Yukon, all the way to Inuvik, in the Northwest Territories, over seven hundred kilometres. The road crosses the Arctic Circle about thirty-five kilometres north of here, and at Eagle Plains you stand on a high plateau of tundra and stunted spruce, with the Richardson Mountains on the horizon to the northeast.

The reason this stop matters is simple: it is the only place on the road with fuel, food and a bed. The hotel and service station are the lifeline of the Dempster, and riders plan their day around it. From Dawson City it is roughly three hundred and seventy kilometres, and to the next fuel at Fort McPherson is some distance more. Fill the tank here, whatever the gauge says. The tyre repair shop has seen every kind of puncture, because the surface is made of sharp shale, and flats are a regular part of life.

The Dempster is named after a Mountie, Inspector William Dempster, who went out in search of a lost patrol of four Royal Northwest Mounted Police officers in 1911. The men, travelling by dog team from Fort McPherson to Dawson, lost their way and died in the cold, and Dempster found their bodies. The highway was built decades later, opened in 1979, and it follows the route of the old dog sled trail. Caribou migrate across the road in some seasons, and wolves, bears, moose and golden eagles are common.

Riding here is a serious job. The gravel can be loose in dry weather and turns into slick mud after rain, and passing trucks throw stones. Weather changes fast, and cold winds blow even in summer. The midnight sun means light for most of the night in June and July, and the autumn colours of the tundra, with red and gold bushes, are lovely in late August. Carry spare tyres or tubes, tools, extra water, food and warm clothes, and leave plenty of time. The silence at the edge of the Arctic is the real prize.
t.town of luang prabang@19.9,102.1:
Before the sun is properly up, a line of monks in saffron robes walks barefoot along the main street of Luang Prabang, and townspeople kneel on mats to put handfuls of sticky rice into their bowls. The alms round, tak bat, is the daily heartbeat of the town, and it has been going on for centuries. Luang Prabang sits on a peninsula where the Nam Khan river meets the Mekong, ringed by green mountains, and for several hundred years it was the royal capital of the Lao kingdom of Lan Xang. The old town, with its gilded temples, wooden houses and French colonial villas, was listed by UNESCO in 1995, and it is one of the best-preserved towns in Southeast Asia.

Wat Xieng Thong, a temple founded in the sixteenth century, has roofs that sweep nearly to the ground and a back wall with a tree of life in glass mosaic. The former Royal Palace is now a museum, and Phou Si, a steep little hill in the centre with a stairway of several hundred steps, gives a view over the rooftops and rivers at sunset, together with a considerable crowd. The night market on the main street sells silk, paper lanterns and hand-woven cloth by lamplight, and fresh baguettes, a French legacy, appear at breakfast with strong Lao coffee.

The riding to get here is a pleasure and a trial. Route 13, the main road north from Vientiane, climbs through mountain forest with endless curves, steep sections and slow lorries, passing the karst country around Vang Vieng. In the wet season, from May to October, landslides and potholes can slow everything. Beyond the town, roads lead north to Nong Khiaw and toward the Chinese border, and the best day trip is to the Kuang Si waterfalls, about thirty kilometres south, whose turquoise pools drop in terraces through the forest.

Luang Prabang, with some forty-seven thousand inhabitants, has fuel, repair shops and plenty of guesthouses. The best season is November to February, when the air is cool and dry. From March to April, farmers burn the fields, and haze can hide the mountains.

Try the local river weed, khai pen, a crisp snack with sesame, and a bowl of khao soi, a noodle soup, at a market stall.
t.ombilin railway@-0.7,100.8:
Few railways in the world have a story as odd as this one. The Ombilin line ran from the coal mines of Sawahlunto in West Sumatra down to the sea at Padang, built by the Dutch in the 1890s to carry coal that colonial industry wanted for ships and engines. To get from the highlands to the coast it had to cross the steep Anai valley, and the engineers solved it with a rack section, a toothed central rail gripped by a cog on the locomotive, the Abt system, which crawls up grades that normal wheels could not hold.

Today parts of the line still survive, and the rest is a ghost of embankments, stations and bridges. Look for the old stations in the highland towns, with their heavy colonial roofs. Steam locomotives, including the famous Mak Itam, have worked tourist trains on the Sawahlunto section, though schedules come and go. The whole railway, together with the mines and the town built around them, was listed by UNESCO in 2019 as a mining heritage landscape.

For a rider the real pleasure is the country the line passes through. This is Minangkabau land: steep green hills, rice terraces, and the cone of Marapi volcano above the clouds. The road from Padang climbs through the Anai gorge, where a waterfall tumbles beside the carriageway, and it is a busy, bendy highway thick with trucks and buses. Take it slowly and early in the day, before afternoon rain, which is regular in this part of Sumatra.

Solok, eighteen kilometres from the site, is a good place for fuel and food, and Sijunjung, a little further, will do if you are heading east. Eat rendang, the slow-cooked beef curry that Minangkabau cooks are famous for, at any of the Padang-style restaurants, which put out dishes on the table and charge only for what you touch.
t.company town@-0.7,100.8:
Sawahlunto is a town built in a bowl, and the company that built it made no secret about who was in charge. After coal was found in the valley in the 1860s, the Dutch colonial government set out to turn a handful of rice fields, which is what Sawahlunto means, into a mining centre, and the town grew up in layers around the pits. The officers' houses sat on the high ground with space and shade, while the labourers' quarters crowded closer to the work.

The people who did the digging were a mixed lot. Many were convicts brought in from Java and elsewhere in the Dutch East Indies, known as orang rantai, the chain people, because they worked in chains. Later, free labourers came from across the archipelago, so the town acquired an odd cultural mix: Minangkabau, Javanese, Chinese, Batak. You can still see it in the streets, the food and the buildings. Dutch-era houses with high ceilings and wide verandas stand beside mosques, and a handsome old power station and station building have been turned into museums.

The coal brought money and power but also hardship. When the mines ran down in the later twentieth century, the town nearly emptied, until it began presenting its history as a reason to visit. In 2019 UNESCO listed the town together with the railway and mining sites as a heritage landscape.

The road to Sawahlunto from Solok, about nineteen kilometres, climbs through green hills and tight bends with a lot of truck traffic. Take it slowly. The town is much quieter than you might expect from the roads. Solok has plenty of fuel and food, and in Sawahlunto itself there are simple eateries, so you can happily take a lunch break among the old company buildings. Wear a rain jacket in the afternoons, because storms build quickly in the hills.
t.soengai doerian mining site@-0.7,100.8:
Soengai Doerian is the old Dutch spelling of Sungai Durian, the river of durians, and the name is one of the nicer details in a story that is mostly about hard labour. The mine here opened in the early years of the Ombilin coalfield, when the colonial government cut shafts into the hillsides around Sawahlunto and dragged out the black seams that fed steamships and railways across the Indies. Of the old workings in the region, this is one of the places where you can feel what the industry actually asked of people.

The coal lay in narrow seams under steep, jungle-covered ridges, and the first miners worked by lamp in tunnels shored up with timber. Convict labour, known locally as the chain people, did much of the early digging, and the mining brought deaths from collapse, gas and fire. A tall chimney, rusted rails and stone retaining walls survive in some of the old compounds, and the engineering of the little tramways that wound down the slopes is a miniature of the larger railway to the coast.

The countryside is greener than you would guess. Banana, cocoa and rubber grow among the old pits, and in the evening, damp mist drifts up the valley. The road from Solok is steep, twisting and pitted in places, with lorries grinding uphill. Heavy rain is common in the afternoon and turns clay verges into slick patches, so aim to arrive in the morning. The cooler, clearer months, roughly June to August, give you the best views.

Solok, about nineteen kilometres off, has fuel and food stalls, and Sijunjung is a similar distance in the other direction. Sawahlunto itself has small restaurants serving Minangkabau dishes, usually rice with a dozen small plates of curry and chilli. If a local offers you durian from a roadside stall, remember that the smell is worse than the taste for many people, but the season is short and the fruit is fabulous.
A coal mine is only half the story. The other half is the machinery that turns raw rock into something a ship can burn, and the processing plant compound at Sawahlunto belongs to that quieter half of the Ombilin heritage. Here coal coming out of the tunnels was sorted, washed and graded before being loaded on wagons and sent down the line toward the port at Padang.

The compound is a collection of brick and iron structures typical of colonial industry in the tropics: tall workshop halls, boiler houses, sheds with heavy roof trusses, and the footings of machines that were once the most advanced equipment in Sumatra. What strikes visitors is the sheer solidity of the construction. Walls are thick, windows are narrow and high, and roofs overhang to keep rain out. The builders obviously expected the plant to last, and it did, long after the coal industry shrank and the pits were abandoned.

The surroundings reward a slow look. Hills crowd in on all sides, covered in dense green, and the humidity gives the air a kind of weight. Old rails still run through weeds, and some wagons have been left as monuments. The best time of year is the drier season between June and September, though rain in Sumatra can arrive in any month with very little warning. Mornings are cooler and better for photos.

On a bike, the road from Solok is a pleasant winding climb through villages and rice paddies, with the usual slow trucks and wandering chickens. Mind the rain-slick edges. Solok, a town of nearly fifty thousand, is the place to fill the tank and buy water, and Sijunjung is useful if you are continuing east. In Sawahlunto town, small cafes sell coffee and fried snacks, and a museum in an old building explains the mining industry in photographs and models. A short visit here pairs well with a walk around the town centre and a glance at the nearby mining school.
t.mining school@-0.7,100.8:
Colonial mining needed more than brute strength. It needed men who could read a gauge, repair a pump and keep records, and so the mining school at Sawahlunto is a small clue to how the Dutch tried to build a local skilled workforce. Education in the Indies was tightly rationed, and a technical school was a rare opening for the sons of Indonesian families, even if the best jobs stayed with European engineers.

The building belongs to a style found across the old town: whitewashed walls, tall shuttered windows, wide verandas to catch breezes and keep out the downpours. Inside such schools the training would have covered drawing, mechanics, basic mathematics and the practicalities of working underground. Walk the surrounding streets and you will see how the school fitted into a planned settlement, with officers' housing, a hospital, a market, and the mine entrances never far away.

There is not much here for those who want drama. The pleasure is in the details: the pattern of the roof tiles, the old iron drains, the stone steps worn smooth. The valley setting, with steep ridges all around and mist rolling down in the evening, is part of the character, and the town is quiet and cool in the early morning. Weekends bring local families, and school groups often come for field trips.

Coming from Solok, the road climbs and twists for about nineteen kilometres through plantations and small villages. Traffic is mostly trucks and scooters, and the surface can be broken at the edges. Wet afternoons are the norm in the wet season, so try to see the site before lunch. Fuel and a proper meal are best sorted in Solok, with a smaller choice in Sawahlunto. The Minangkabau dish of rendang, dark with spices and cooked down for hours, is a good reward after a day among the colonial buildings.
t.coal storage@-1.0,100.4:
Coal needs a harbour, and for the Ombilin mines the harbour was at Padang, on Sumatra's west coast, about five kilometres from the site. The Dutch built a deep-water port in the bay south of the town, naming it Emmahaven after the queen consort, and the railway from Sawahlunto ended here at the quay and the storage yards. Today the port is known as Teluk Bayur, and some of the old coal-handling structures can still be seen.

Piles of coal were stocked in sheds and yards before loading onto ships bound for bunkers around the Indian Ocean, and the infrastructure of the quay, railway sidings and warehouses is part of the heritage listing. The location tells a larger story: Sumatra's interior wealth went to the coast by rail, and from there to the wider empire's engines. Standing in the yard, with cranes and container stacks beyond, you get a sense of how long this shore has been in the business of moving heavy cargo.

Padang is a lively, hot, humid city of around eight hundred thousand people, and the sea breeze is welcome after the highlands. The ride to the coast from Padang Panjang descends the Anai valley, a good road with plenty of bends, trucks and the roar of water over rocks. Early morning keeps the traffic down. Afternoon downpours are the rule, so keep your rain gear handy. The coast road has fewer curves but more traffic and some potholes.

Fuel is no problem in Padang, with stations on every main road, and restaurants offer the full Minangkabau menu. Try a plate of nasi padang with spicy fish and green chilli sambal. The city also sits in an active earthquake zone, and the memory of the 2009 quake is part of local life, so ask locally about road conditions before any long trip. Solok, a long way inland, is the next large fuel stop after the highlands.
t.kayu tanam train station@-0.5,100.3:
Kayu Tanam is a small mountain-foot town on the old road and railway between Padang and the highlands of West Sumatra, the place where the flat coastal plain gives up and the Bukit Barisan range begins. The station is a relic of the Dutch era, when the colonial railway pushed inland to bring coal from the Ombilin mines at Sawahlunto down to the port at Padang. The line climbed the steep Anai gorge and, higher up, used a toothed rack rail to manage the gradient, and the whole system was recognised by UNESCO in 2019 as part of the Ombilin coal mining heritage.

Today the road beside the line is the more interesting ride. The Padang to Bukittinggi highway squeezes through the Anai valley, a green slot where a waterfall called Lembah Anai drops almost to the verge and where on wet days mist drifts across the carriageway. t.pua@19.2,100.9:

t.bo kluea@19.2,101.2:

t.phitsanulok@16.8,100.3:

t.padang@-0.9,100.4:

t.megalithic jar sites in xiengkhuang plai:

t.saloum delta@13.8,-16.5:

t.site 42@19.6,103.6:

The jars are carved from sandstone, granite or limestone, many of them taller than a person, and they date from the Iron Age, roughly two thousand years ago. Archaeologists found human bones and burial goods around them, and the usual theory is that they were part of funeral rites, perhaps used to hold bodies until the bones could be buried. Who made them is still not well understood.

t.site 2@19.3,103.2:

t.fort bullen@13.5,-16.5:

t.site 52@19.5,103.4:

t.padang pandjang train station@-0.5,100.4:
