Traffic is heavy with lorries, buses and motorbikes, and the surface is often damaged by rain, so take care, especially in the wet. The mornings are best, since clouds and rain gather in the afternoon, and the fog on the upper section can be thick.

Bukittinggi, about seventeen kilometres away, is the main town of the highlands, with fuel, cafes and plenty of places to stay, and Padang Panjang itself has stations and shops. Keep an eye on the volcano: Marapi is active and sometimes closed to climbers because of eruptions.
t.ombilin coal mining heritage of sawahlun:
Sawahlunto sits in a steep green bowl in the hills of West Sumatra, and until the 1890s there was nothing here but forest and a few villages. Then the Dutch found out what lay beneath. A Dutch geologist, Willem Hendrik de Greve, surveyed the Ombilin valley and reported a huge coal deposit in 1868, and the colonial government decided to exploit it, building a mine, a railway down to the coast at Padang, and a town to house the workers. The first coal went out in 1892. The town grew around the mine, with European quarters, a power station, a hospital, a mosque and houses laid out on the hillsides.

The human cost of that history needs to be told. Many of the labourers were convicts, brought from Java and elsewhere and known as the orang rantai, the chain men, who worked in the dark tunnels in terrible conditions. The Mbah Soero tunnel, named after a foreman of the convict gangs, can still be visited. UNESCO listed the Ombilin coal mining heritage of Sawahlunto in 2019, with the railway and the port, for its testimony to the way colonial industry shaped the landscape and the people.

Sawahlunto now has the air of a town that has reinvented itself. The mines closed, and the old buildings have been turned into museums, including a railway museum and a goedang ransum, the old mass kitchen that fed the miners, and the old locomotives are a favourite attraction. The little town is quiet and clean, with hills all around and a fresh breeze, and the pace of life is gentle.

The road from Solok, about ten kilometres to the west, is a pleasure on a bike. It runs past Lake Singkarak, a large, deep lake in a volcanic basin, with fishing boats and views of misty hills, and climbs and falls with plenty of bends. Traffic can be heavy with trucks and buses, and the road surface varies, with patches broken by rain. The dry months from May to September offer the best conditions, though showers can come at any time in the tropics.

Solok, with about forty-eight thousand people, has fuel, restaurants and hotels, and the town of Sijunjung, farther east, is smaller. Try the local fish from the lake, and the rice dishes of the Minangkabau kitchen, hot with chilli.
t.tinggi bridge@-0.5,100.4:
Sumatra's western highlands are the home of the Minangkabau, a matrilineal people whose houses have roofs curved like buffalo horns, and the road up from the coast at Padang to the cool plateau around Bukittinggi is one of the great short climbs in Indonesia. It passes through the Anai valley, past a waterfall that falls close to the roadside, and through the little railway halt of Kayu Tanam, where the old line from Padang once began its steep ascent on its way to the Ombilin coal fields. That railway, built by the Dutch in the late nineteenth century with a rack section to climb the grade, is now part of the UNESCO-listed Ombilin Coal Mining Heritage of Sawahlunto.

The bridge sits in this corridor, within sight of the tracks and the river, and shows how the engineers of the time threaded a hard-won line between rock face and gorge. The valley is deeply green, with banana plants, cinnamon trees, rice terraces and mist hanging on the slopes in the morning. Two volcanoes, Marapi and Singgalang, stand over the plateau, and on a clear day they are magnificent.

On a motorcycle, the climb from the coast is a pleasure and a test. The road is a main route, with a mix of good asphalt and patched sections, plenty of bends, and heavy truck and bus traffic that overtakes on corners with great confidence. Small motorcycles are everywhere, and drivers expect you to be flexible. Rain arrives most afternoons, and the surface can be greasy under leaf litter. The best hours are early, before the buses fill the road, and the drier months from May to September.

The nearest big town is Bukittinggi, about nineteen kilometres from here, a lively hill town with fuel, markets, a clock tower, and good local food. Try rendang, the slow-cooked beef curry that the Minangkabau made famous, at a Padang restaurant where plates arrive without ordering and you pay for what you eat. Coffee is grown on the slopes and served strong and sweet. Fuel stations dot the main road, but the little villages in the valley may have only roadside sellers with bottles, so top up in Bukittinggi or Padang Panjang.
t.remains of portuguese chapel@13.3,-16.4:
The Gambia is a country shaped like a river, a ribbon of land on either bank of a wide, slow stream that cuts deep into Senegal, and Albreda is a village on the north bank that tells the story of why Europeans came. The Portuguese were the first, in the fifteenth century, trading with the peoples of the river, and the remains of their chapel, a ruined stone and brick shell, stand among the houses. The French set up a trading post at Albreda in the seventeenth century, and the British, who held James Island, now Kunta Kinteh Island, a short boat ride away, fought them for control of the river trade. The trade was in gold, ivory, hides and, increasingly, human beings, and the slave trade from this stretch of the Gambia lasted some three centuries. UNESCO listed Kunta Kinteh Island and Related Sites in 2003.

The neighbouring village of Juffureh is where the writer Alex Haley traced the ancestry in his book Roots, and a small museum records the story. Walking through the village, with its market, children and baobab trees, is moving and complicated. People here are friendly and open, and a local guide can explain how the history is lived.

Getting to this side of the river means crossing it. The ferry between Banjul and Barra is a crowded and slow experience, with long queues and unpredictable timetables, and I would plan a couple of hours for the crossing, with some patience. From Barra, the road runs east along the north bank, with sandy verges, goats and children, and the surface varies from good to rutted and pot-holed. Traffic is light, with bush taxis, donkey carts and the odd lorry. The best season is from November to April, when the air is dry and warm and the harmattan wind brings a haze, and the rains from July to September make unpaved side roads difficult.

Fuel is available at Barra and larger towns like Farafenni, further up the north bank, but may be scarce or inconsistent in villages, so fill up whenever you can and carry a spare can. Bring cash in dalasi, because cards are rarely accepted, and drink bottled water.

The ride list goes on to the Saloum Delta in Senegal, a maze of mangroves and shell islands on the coast, and the roads between the two countries cross a border that can take time.
t.stone circles of senegambia@13.7,-15.5:
The Gambia is a thin green country, shaped like a tongue lolling out of Senegal along the river that gives it its name, and its most intriguing monuments are its stones. Near Kerbatch, in the Central River Region, a group of circles of tall laterite pillars stands in open woodland, each circle made of upright stones as tall as a person, shaped by hand and set in a ring. They belong to the stone circles of Senegambia, which spread across the lands on both sides of the border, and number in the thousands, with several different groups listed together as a World Heritage property in 2006. The tradition of putting up such circles seems to have lasted from about the third century BC until the sixteenth century.

Nobody knows exactly who built them, but excavations suggest that they were funerary monuments for important people, each with burials beneath or beside the stones, and that the builders were an organised society with iron tools and a well-developed trade network. The laterite was quarried in blocks and trimmed into pillars, and some of the stones weigh several tonnes. The stones are red-brown, pitted and warm to the touch in the afternoon, and they stand in long grass with shea and baobab trees, the sort of place where you walk quietly.

The road here is the Trans-Gambia Highway, which connects the north and south banks of the river, and its quality has improved in recent years with a bridge across the Gambia at Farafenni, opened in 2019, that replaced a slow and unpredictable ferry. The riding is flat, hot and mostly straight, with goats, cattle and donkeys always liable to wander across, and shared taxis that stop without warning. Police checkpoints are frequent and usually friendly, so carry your documents and a smile. The best time is the dry season, from November to February, with cooler mornings, though in the harmattan season dust haze hangs over the land.

Farafenni, a lively trading town of nearly thirty thousand people sixteen kilometres away, has fuel stations, a big market and basic hotels, so fill the tank there before you turn off. Nearby villages have small shops with soft drinks, bread and sweet tea, and in the evenings you will hear drums. Carry water and a hat, and carry some small notes, since change can be scarce. A guide at the stones will add to your visit, and a small fee is expected.
t.wanar@13.9,-15.6:
The strangest stones in Africa may be the lyre-shaped ones at Wanar. The site, in the Sine-Saloum region of central Senegal, is among the largest groups of megaliths on the continent, with dozens of circles made of tall, rounded laterite pillars, and among them stand a few unusual forked stones, shaped like a lyre or a letter Y, with a notch cut in the top. Archaeologists think they were made by deliberately splitting the stone, and the form seems to echo the shape of a branched tree. Nobody can say for sure what the shape meant, which is part of the appeal. The stones at Wanar form part of the Senegambian stone circles, listed as World Heritage in 2006.

The setting is the peanut basin, a flat, sandy country with fields of groundnuts and millet, scattered baobab and acacia trees, and villages of mud-brick and thatch, where groups of women pound grain in the early morning. Dry season, from November to May, makes the landscape pale and dusty, with a golden haze, and the rains from July to October turn it a deep green. Sereer and Wolof people live here, and the village near the stones takes care of the site.

On a motorbike, Senegal's roads are manageable, but they require alertness. The main highways are paved and generally good, with long straight stretches, while the minor roads are often sandy, with deep corrugations and drifts, so a light touch and steady speed are needed. Donkey carts, bush taxis and herds of goats are common hazards, and nighttime riding is unwise, since vehicles often lack lights. Police checkpoints are frequent, and it is useful to carry copies of your documents. The heat can be intense in the hot months, from March to June, and the best time to ride is between December and February.

Nioro du Rip, twenty-three kilometres away, is a market town of about twenty thousand with fuel stations, small shops and basic lodging, and Kaolack, a bigger city to the west, offers a wider choice. Local food includes millet porridge, rice with fish and the thick peanut stew called mafe, and the sweet, spiced hibiscus drink, bissap, is a good way to cool down. Carry plenty of water and expect to be greeted warmly by the children who come out to see the visitors.
t.james island@13.3,-16.4:
A rock in the Gambia river has been renamed three times, and each name tells you a chapter. In 1651, the Duchy of Courland, a small Baltic state, built a fort on the island and called it St Andrew's. The British took it ten years later and renamed it James Island, after the Duke of York, and it passed back and forth between the British, French and pirates, a base for the trade in enslaved Africans, and later a fort and a mission. In 2011 the Gambian government renamed it Kunta Kinteh Island, after the hero of Alex Haley's novel Roots, who is said to have been taken from the village of Juffureh on the riverbank, close by. Whether or not the story of Kunta Kinte is literally true, the island has become a powerful symbol of the slave trade, and the ruins of the fort, with its crumbling walls and cannons, are a sober sight. The island and the related sites on the shore were listed as a World Heritage property in 2003.

The island is small, and it is getting smaller, with erosion by the river eating away at the walls, and visits are made by boat from Albreda, the village on the north bank. The villages of Juffureh and Albreda have a museum about the slave trade, with chains and records, and a few craft stalls. The surrounding country is the Saloum delta region, a maze of mangrove channels, mudflats and low islands, where fishermen set nets and oyster gatherers wade at low tide, and the birdlife is rich, with pelicans, herons and kingfishers.

Getting there involves a ferry. From Banjul, the capital, the Barra ferry crosses the wide mouth of the river, and the queue for vehicles can be long, with delays of hours at peak times. On the north bank, the road to Albreda runs through villages and baobab groves, flat and hot, with goats, children and the occasional pothole. Take care at the ferry terminal, which is chaotic. The best months are November to February, when the weather is dry and cooler.

Lamin, about nine kilometres from the island on the map, is the nearest sizeable settlement, and is on the south bank, near Serrekunda. Fuel is available around Banjul and Barra, but supplies can be unreliable in the country, so fill up when you can. Carry water, sun protection and insect repellent, and small notes for the boatman. A grilled fish and a cold drink in a village bar finish the day well, and the sunset over the river can be spectacular.
t.arctic circle@66.6,-136.3:
The Arctic Circle is a line that doesn't exist, and yet people stop for it. On the Dempster Highway there is a rest area at the point where the road crosses 66 degrees 33 minutes north, with a sign, a board of information, and a gravel parking pad. It is not a dramatic place, apart from the landscape: a wide valley of tundra, scrubby spruce and low hills, with the Richardson Mountains on the far horizon. Above this line, in midsummer, the sun does not set.

The Dempster is one of the great gravel roads of North America, and it is not for the faint-hearted. It runs about 740 kilometres from near Dawson City in the Yukon to Inuvik in the Northwest Territories, built up on a thick gravel bed to protect the permafrost. The surface is mostly hard-packed, but it can be slippery after rain, sharp with stones, and rough with washboard. Flat tyres are routine, so carry a spare and a repair kit. Trucks throw stones, so give them room.

There is no town near the Arctic Circle marker. Fuel is at Eagle Plains, a lonely lodge with a hotel, restaurant and garage, which is the only service for hundreds of kilometres in the Yukon, and the next fuel is in Fort McPherson. Fill up everywhere, carry extra fuel if you can, and check road conditions before you leave, since rain and snow can close the road quickly. Ferries cross the Peel and Mackenzie rivers in summer, and the schedule changes with the weather and the ice.

This is caribou and bear country, and the light in June and July is soft and endless. Mosquitoes can be dense, so bring repellent and a head net. The summer window is short, usually from June to early September, and the road is a lonely one, so tell someone your plan and carry water and food.
t.kong lor cave@18.0,104.7:
The Nam Hin Bun river does something rivers rarely do: it walks straight into a mountain and comes out the other side. At Kong Lor, in the Khammouane province of central Laos, it flows into a limestone tunnel about seven kilometres long, passing beneath the great karst ridge of the Phu Hin Bun, and visitors can travel through it in long narrow boats with outboard motors, in near-total darkness, with only a headlamp to light the way. The cave roof rises as high as ninety metres in places, and the formations, in places lit by coloured lamps, are impressive.

The trip takes an hour or two in all, and at the far end, the boat emerges into a green valley, with a rest stop where you can wait for the return. In the dry season, from November to April, the water is shallow in places, and passengers may have to get out and wade while the boatman drags the boat over rocks. In the rainy season the river is fuller but also stronger. Tickets are bought in the village of Ban Kong Lor, and a guide goes with each boat. The cave is spectacular, and the silence between engine noises is deep.

The Thakhek Loop, of which this is the finish, is one of the great motorcycle journeys of Southeast Asia, a circuit of around four hundred kilometres through limestone mountains, rice valleys, rivers and villages. The roads vary from smooth asphalt to broken surface and gravel, and the scenery is wild and beautiful, with green cliffs rising out of the paddies. Traffic is light, the people are friendly, and the pace is relaxed. Water buffalo, dogs and chickens share the road, so slow down.

Practical matters need some planning. The nearest town of any size is Ban Nahin, on the main road, where you can find fuel, food and basic repairs, and it is wise to fill the tank there. In small villages along the loop, petrol is sold from bottles at roadside stalls, and while it works in an emergency, quality varies. Carry water, cash in Lao kip, and a rain jacket. Mobile signal is patchy in the valleys. Guesthouses at Ban Kong Lor offer simple rooms and meals of sticky rice, grilled fish and spicy dips, and the sound of the river at night is a pleasant lullaby. Rain in the wet season, from May to October, can make the roads muddy.
t.encumeada pass@32.8,-17.0:
Encumeada is the notch in Madeira's spine where the island shows both of its faces at once. At just over a thousand metres, the pass sits between the high peaks that run east to west, and from the viewpoint beside the road you can look north to the valley that falls toward São Vicente and south to the valley of Ribeira Brava, with the sea glinting in each direction when the cloud permits. On a clear day it feels almost like standing on a roof.

The road here, the ER228, is one of the island's classics. Coming up from the south it climbs through terraced farms, eucalyptus and pine, and hairpins carry you up to the saddle; on the north side the descent is steeper and more dramatic, with tunnels drilled through rock and waterfalls pouring down cliffs beside the road. Surfaces are mostly good, but expect damp patches and falling stones in wet weather, and watch for fog, which can drop onto the pass in minutes and turn the road to a grey tunnel. Morning tends to be clearest, with cloud building from midday as the sun heats the slopes.

Beyond the road, the pass is a jumping-off point for walking. Levadas, the narrow irrigation channels built centuries ago to carry water from the wet north to the dry south, run through the mountain forest, and several famous trails start near here. The laurel forests of Madeira, which are a UNESCO World Heritage site, grow in the damp folds of these mountains, and the smell of wet earth and leaves is part of the place. The island's mountains were built by volcanoes, and the cliffs beside the road show layers of ash and lava in rust and grey.

There is a small kiosk or café at the pass in season and a car park by the viewpoint, but for fuel you need to descend to São Vicente on the north coast or Ribeira Brava to the south. Carry a rain jacket and a warm layer, since the temperature drops at altitude and the wind can be fierce. In the summer months the pass is a lovely cool place to stop, and a hot coffee tastes better here than almost anywhere.

Take a moment at the viewpoint to look both ways before you choose which side of the island to drop into.
t.paul da serra@32.8,-17.1:
Paul da Serra is the odd one out in Madeira, because it is flat. After the steep valleys and hairpins of the coast, you climb onto a high plateau about fourteen hundred metres up where the land spreads out into open moorland of heather, gorse and tussock grass, with a few cattle and sheep and a scatter of wind turbines. It feels like Scotland dropped into the Atlantic, and the first time you reach it you wonder where the subtropical island has gone.

The name means something like the marsh of the mountain, and it earns it. The plateau catches the clouds that roll up from the sea, absorbs the rain and feeds the springs and streams that supply Madeira's levada network of irrigation channels. In wet weather the ground is soaked, and fog can fall so thickly that visibility drops to a few metres. When the sky is clear the views are enormous, with the Atlantic stretching away on both sides and the peaks of the central massif lined up to the east. The air is cool, the wind is steady, and the light is wide and bright.

The road across, the ER209, is one of the best on the island for riding: long straight stretches broken by smooth, wide bends, hardly any traffic, and an open feeling that contrasts with the narrow coastal lanes. Take care, though. Fog, wind, and sheep and cattle on the road are all real hazards, and in winter there can be ice or even a dusting of snow. Late spring and autumn usually bring the best weather, and early morning is quietest.

Beyond the plateau, side roads lead down to places like Rabaçal and the laurel forest of Fanal, where ancient trees stand wrapped in moss and mist. The laurisilva forest, a relic of the vegetation that once covered southern Europe, is protected and listed by UNESCO, and walking in it is an experience you will remember.

There are almost no services on the plateau. Fuel stations are in the towns on the coast, such as Calheta or São Vicente, and it is wise to fill up before you climb. Carry water, a rain jacket and a warm layer, and keep your phone charged in case the weather turns. The silence here, broken only by wind and distant bells, is the real treat.
t.camara de lobos@32.6,-17.0:
Câmara de Lobos is the fishing harbour everyone paints. Winston Churchill sat here in 1950 to do exactly that, on a holiday to Madeira, and the place still trades on the connection with a viewpoint named after him. Below the road, a small bay of brightly painted wooden boats, drying nets and stone steps looks very much as it must have done a century ago, and above it white houses climb the slope in terraces.

The name means chamber of the wolves, and the wolves in question were monk seals, which the Portuguese navigator João Gonçalves Zarco found sleeping here in the early fifteenth century when he explored the island. The seals are almost gone from Madeira now, but the fishermen are not. They go out at night after espada, the black scabbardfish, a long, silvery, rather alarming-looking deep-sea fish that is served fried with banana, a combination that sounds odd and tastes excellent. The harbour smells of diesel, salt and grilled fish, which is exactly what it should.

For riders, the town is a gateway. It lies just west of Funchal on the south coast and acts as a springboard for the roads up into the hills, including the climb to the cliff of Cabo Girão and the winding lanes that run through banana plantations and vineyards. In the town itself the streets are narrow and steep, parking is tight, and traffic gets busy around the harbour, so take it slowly and watch for locals stepping out between parked cars. The best moment is early morning, when the boats come in and the light is soft, or at sunset when the bay turns gold.

Fuel and food are no problem. With more than thirty thousand people in the municipality and the capital almost next door, Câmara de Lobos has petrol stations, supermarkets and plenty of cafés. The local drink is poncha, a strong mix of sugar cane spirit, honey and lemon juice, mixed with a wooden stick called a mexedor; take it in small sips, particularly if you are riding afterwards, which is a sound reason to try it at the end of the day instead.

Sit with a coffee by the water for a while. The harbour is small, but the mood and the colours are worth a few minutes of your day.
t.cabo girao@32.7,-17.0:
At Cabo Girão the land simply stops. A cliff drops almost six hundred metres straight into the Atlantic, one of the highest sea cliffs in Europe, and a glass-floored skywalk juts out from the rim so you can look straight down at the waves, the little farms and the red roofs of the fajãs at the bottom. Those narrow flat patches at the foot of the cliff, formed by old landslides, are farmed by people who once reached them only by boat or by steep paths, and today a small cable car also serves them.

Looking down from the platform is a mildly queasy pleasure. Terraced plots of vegetables, grapevines and bananas cling to the ledges, and tiny figures work among them. Looking out, you see the south coast of Madeira curving away toward Funchal, the water changing from deep blue to green near the rocks. Early morning gives the best light and the least cloud, and calm days let you hear the sea far below, a faint rumble like traffic.

The ride in is straightforward. From Câmara de Lobos, a few kilometres east, you climb a well-paved road through villages and plantations, with a succession of bends and fine views of the coast. The car park by the viewpoint fills with coaches in the middle of the day, so arrive early or late. Gusts can be strong near the edge, so take care with your helmet and anything you place on a bike. The glass section of the skywalk can be unsettling if you do not like heights, but the railings are solid and the experience is safe.

There is a café near the viewpoint and a small shop, but you should carry water and some cash. Fuel is available at Câmara de Lobos, only a few kilometres away, and at Ribeira Brava to the west, so there is no need to worry. Weather on Madeira changes fast, and cloud can sweep across the cliff, so check conditions before you commit.

The cliff has long been a landmark for sailors, and the name is sometimes explained as a reference to a navigator who turned back here, although the exact origin is uncertain. Whatever the story, the sense of space is the thing you remember.
t.doi phu kha@19.2,101.1:
Northern Nan province is the Thailand most people never see: long ridges folded one behind another, forest the colour of wet slate, and villages where the language, the clothes and the food change from one valley to the next. Doi Phu Kha sits in the middle of it, inside a national park that covers the highest mountains in the province and runs close to the Laos border. The coordinates here sit at about 1,715 metres, high enough for mist to pool in the valleys at dawn and for the evenings to turn properly cold between December and February.

The park is known for plants, and it is one of the places where you can see wild Himalayan cherry blossom in Thailand. The trees flower pink in the cool season, usually around the turn of the year, and when they do, a few lucky weeks bring Thai visitors in the thousands. The forest is a mix of evergreen hill forest, oak and pine, with orchids, ferns and rhododendron, and the air smells of damp earth and resin. Hill peoples including Hmong, Mien and Lua have lived on these slopes for generations, and their villages cling to terraces and clearings. A greeting and a smile go a long way, and photographing people calls for asking first.

The riding up here is the draw. The roads in northern Nan are narrow, steep and twisty, some of the finest in Thailand, and traffic is almost non-existent. Bends tighten and the surface can be broken in places, with patches of gravel or mud after rain, and cattle sometimes wander across the road. The rainy season, roughly from June to October, brings landslides and slick surfaces, and the cool dry months from November to February are the best for riding, though mornings can be cold and misty. Be careful on the downhills, where brakes work hard.

Services are sparse. Chiang Klang, about twenty-six kilometres away, is the nearest town with proper petrol stations and shops, so fill the tank there and carry water and snacks before heading into the park. Small village stalls may sell noodles or sticky rice with grilled pork, and park accommodation is simple, with basic bungalows and camping. A rain jacket and a warm layer are not optional.

Start early, take your time, and leave daylight for the way back. Phone signal can disappear in the valleys, and the mountain dark falls quickly once the sun drops behind the ridge.
t.santikhiri road@19.0,101.0:
The road threads through the mountains of Nan province near the Laotian frontier, and it is one of those routes that makes you slow down simply to look. The label here is Santikhiri road, and the coordinates put it among forested ridges north of the small town of Chiang Klang, with nothing larger than a village for many kilometres. What you can say honestly about this country is that it is wild, empty and beautiful, and that riding it is a pleasure in the old sense of the word.

The landscape is rolling mountain forest, with teak, oak and bamboo on the lower slopes and cooler, mossy woods above. Hill villages appear in clearings, with wooden houses on stilts, rice drying on mats, chickens and pigs wandering across the road, and smoke rising from kitchens. This is a mixed corner of Thailand, with ethnic groups such as Hmong, Mien, Lua and Thai Lue living side by side, and the markets and festivals reflect that. Around the turn of the year, wild cherry trees flower on the high ridges in the north of the province, which brings a flush of pink to the hillsides.

Riding conditions change with the season. In the cool, dry months, from about November to February, the air is clear and the mornings are cold, with mist lying in the valleys until the sun burns it away. This is the best time, with firm surfaces and wide views. In the rainy season the road can be slippery, with mud, fallen branches and sometimes landslides, and the leeches come out in the woods. The bends are tight and the gradients steep, with frequent blind corners, so ride within your sight and keep to your side, because trucks and pickups swing wide on the corners.

Facilities are thin. Chiang Klang, about thirty-three kilometres away, and Nan city, a little farther, are the nearest places to fill the tank and buy supplies, so do not set out on a low tank. Small shops in villages sell water, snacks and sometimes fuel in bottles, but quality varies. Carry a spare tube or a repair kit if you have one, because a puncture a long way from anywhere is a slow business.

Stop in a village if you can, have a bowl of noodles and an iced tea, and listen to the quiet. The people are friendly, and a few words of Thai, such as thank you, make a difference.
t.encumeada@32.8,-17.0:
Encumeada is the pass that cuts Madeira in two. At about a thousand metres, it sits on the island's spine between São Vicente on the north coast and Serra de Água on the south, and from the viewpoint at the top you can look down both valleys at once. On a clear day you see the sea on each side, the north in a haze of cloud and the south in sun, with steep green ridges folding away like crumpled cloth. It is one of the few spots on the island where you can feel its shape in a single glance.

The island's wild interior is home to the laurisilva, an ancient laurel forest that once covered much of southern Europe and survives here in a damp, mossy form. Its wet, twisted trees were recognised by UNESCO in 1999, and walkers use the levadas, narrow irrigation channels cut into the mountainsides, to reach waterfalls and viewpoints. Some routes begin near the pass, and the ground drips even on days of sun. The air smells of earth, leaf and rain.

For riders, the road to Encumeada is a mix of tunnels, tight bends and long climbs. From São Vicente it rises along a valley with steep drops, passing waterfalls and terraced fields, and the surface is generally good but can be wet and slippery. Clouds often settle on the pass, reducing visibility, and the temperature falls noticeably compared with the coast. The road demands attention, with sharp corners, short tunnels and the occasional rockfall after heavy rain. On the south side it descends in a series of hairpins to the Ribeira Brava valley, with the views opening toward the sea.

Fuel is not available at the pass, so fill up in São Vicente, about five kilometres away, or in Ribeira Brava on the south coast. A small café and a shop at the viewpoint sell drinks and snacks, though the hours vary. São Vicente is also known for its volcanic caves and a small old town with a chapel set into the rock, and it has several restaurants serving fresh fish, espetada, beef skewers grilled over laurel wood, and bolo do caco, a round bread served with garlic butter.

The weather can change in minutes, from sun to mist to rain, so bring a rain layer and take it slowly. The best light is in the morning, before clouds build on the ridges, and the view from the top is worth the effort.
t.thakhek@17.4,104.8:
Thakhek is a sleepy Mekong river town in central Laos, and it is the traditional starting point of the Thakhek Loop, one of the great motorcycle routes in Southeast Asia. The town sits on the Lao bank of the river, facing the Thai city of Nakhon Phanom across the water, a ferry ride or a short hop over the Friendship Bridge. Old French colonial shophouses line the riverfront in faded yellows and greys, a reminder of the time when this was an administrative outpost of French Indochina. In the evening the promenade fills with locals jogging, playing takraw and eating grilled fish.

The loop itself runs for roughly four hundred kilometres in a circle through Khammouane province, and most riders take three or four days. It starts on Route 13, then turns east on Route 12 into a landscape of limestone karst, tall grey and green towers that rise sharply from rice paddies. The road to Mahaxay and beyond is quiet and well surfaced, with sweeping views, and it leads toward the Nakai plateau and its huge reservoir, created by the Nam Theun 2 dam. The route then returns west through the village of Konglor, home to a river cave about seven kilometres long, where a boat takes you through darkness lit only by your headlamp.

Conditions vary. Some sections are good tarmac, others are patchy or have been damaged by rain, and landslides and potholes appear in the wet season. Fuel is available in Thakhek and in a few larger villages, but stations get far apart on the plateau. Carry some extra and fill whenever you can. Rental bikes are easy to arrange in town, from small automatics to trail machines, and many shops will offer maps and tips.

Food is simple and good: sticky rice, grilled chicken, laap, a minced meat salad with herbs and lime, and cold Beerlao in the evening. Guesthouses along the route are basic and cheap. The best season is November to February, when the air is dry and cool. From June to September the rains bring slippery roads and leeches in the forest.
t.site 3 group 5@19.3,103.2:
Site 3 is the third of the Plain of Jars locations near Phonsavan, in Xieng Khouang province in northern Laos, and it is probably the most attractive to visit. The jars, giant stone vessels carved from sandstone, lie scattered across low grassy hills, and at Site 3 there are over a hundred of them spread across several groups. Group 5 sits on a gentle hillside among rice paddies and is a small cluster, reached by a short walk through farmland. The jars are not uniform, some tall and wide with lips, others broken or toppled, and many tilt as if the ground has been shifting under them for centuries.

Nobody is entirely sure what they were for. The French archaeologist Madeleine Colani worked here in the 1930s and concluded that they were part of a funeral tradition, probably used to hold bodies during decomposition before the bones were buried, and later work has backed her idea. They date to the Iron Age, roughly from 500 BC to 500 AD. Local legend says a giant king brewed rice wine in them after a great victory, and the story is told with a smile.

The landscape has its darker part. Laos was bombed heavily during the Vietnam War by the United States, and the province of Xieng Khouang suffered more than most. Unexploded ordnance remains in the soil. At the jar sites, the safe paths have been cleared and are marked with white and red stones, so stay on the white side and do not wander. The clearing work by MAG and HALO is ongoing and visible, and it is an important part of why this heritage is open to visit.

Phonsavan is about seventeen kilometres away. It is a plain, modern town on a plateau at about a thousand metres, cool in the evenings, with fuel stations, noodle shops and a few places to stay. The road from the town runs through rolling pine and grass hills, with a road surface that is mostly good. Mornings are often misty, especially from December to February, and the light is lovely over the jars. Come early, bring water, and take your time.
t.site 3 groups 1 3@19.3,103.2:
Groups 1 and 3 at Site 3 are two clusters among several that make up this part of the Plain of Jars, near Phonsavan in Xieng Khouang, and they reward patience more than the headline site does. The walking route links the groups through fields and across low ridges, so you move from one cluster to the next with a view over farmland between. Buffaloes graze in the stubble, children cycle past, and the jars appear in the grass ahead like a set of oversized tea cups left from a giant's picnic. The stone is rough sandstone, and lichen has coloured the surfaces in grey and orange patches.

Many of the jars have rims shaped for lids, and a few lids lie near them, carved with simple forms. Some jars show animal figures or masks cut into their sides, though such details are rare. Archaeologists found human bone fragments, beads and ceramics around the sites, which adds weight to the idea that the jars belonged to a funeral practice. No settlement has been found nearby, and the people who made them remain a mystery. Quarry sites where the stone was cut have been identified on hillsides some kilometres away, and moving such heavy blocks must have taken enormous labour.

You will need to take the history of this land seriously. The American bombing campaign of the 1960s and early 1970s left Laos with a legacy of unexploded munitions, and some craters remain visible on the plain, grassed over and filled with water. Respect the markers on the paths. Do not step beyond them, do not pick things up, and listen to local guides.

The nearest town is Phonsavan, with all the fuel and food you need. The plain is a high plateau with cool nights and a clear air, and the best months are from October to March. Roads leading out are mainly paved and gentle, and traffic is light. The hills near the sites are covered in grass and low pine, and the colour of the earth is a soft red. Late afternoon light brings warmth to the stone.
t.site 3 group 4@19.3,103.2:
Group 4 is one of the quieter parts of Site 3, and what makes it worth the walk is its position. The jars here sit on a slight rise with open views over the valley, so that on a clear day you can see across the rice fields and low hills to the line of the horizon. It feels more private than other sites on the plain, with fewer visitors and less sense of being on a trail. The jars are scattered across the grass in an irregular pattern, and a couple are heavily tilted or cracked, which gives the place a worn, old feeling.

The word plain is slightly misleading. The Plain of Jars is really a high plateau, around a thousand metres above sea level, set among taller hills of the Annamite chain. That altitude keeps the air cool and clear, with mist in the early mornings and, in December and January, chilly nights where a jacket is welcome. The soil is red and the vegetation is mostly grass and small pines, with rice paddies in the valleys and patches of teak and bamboo around villages. Hmong and Lao Phuan communities live in the district, and the Phuan are the traditional people of the old kingdom of Xieng Khouang.

Old Muang Khoun, the former capital, lies not far to the south, and it was heavily bombed in the war. A few stupas and a ruined temple remain, and they tell the story better than any museum. In Phonsavan, the Mines Advisory Group runs an information centre that explains the unexploded ordnance problem and the clearance effort, which is worth an hour.

Phonsavan is about eighteen kilometres from the site, with fuel stations, a market, and noodle shops that serve a good pho. The ride out from the town is on well-sealed roads with gentle gradients, and you rarely meet heavy traffic. The best months are October to March. In the wet season, red mud covers the tracks to the jar sites, and the going is slow. Wear sturdy shoes, bring a hat and water, and stay on the cleared paths.
t.site 8@19.3,103.2:
Site 8 is among the smaller and less visited locations connected to the Plain of Jars, in the hills near Phonsavan in northern Laos, and it is less a destination than a reminder that the jars are not confined to three famous sites. Researchers have recorded more than ninety sites across the province, and many hold only a handful of jars, scattered on a hilltop or half-sunk in a field. Few of them are cleared for visitors, so the best way to see lesser sites is through local guides and the organised access that the heritage authorities provide.

That caution matters. Unexploded ordnance from the war years still lies in the ground across Xieng Khouang, and many sites have only partially been cleared. Local people know their land, but a visitor should never walk off a marked path, and nobody should go to an unmarked site alone. The clearing teams place red and white markers along safe routes, and those colours are worth learning before you set out.

The country around is a rolling plateau of grass, pine and farmland. From Phonsavan the roads fan out in several directions, and the one heading southwest toward the jar sites is smooth and quiet. Along the way, you pass small villages with wooden houses on stilts, buffalo wallowing in ponds, and women selling vegetables at roadside stalls. Weather can change quickly, and in the cool season a morning mist rolls across the hills and lifts around nine.

Distances are short but the pace of life is slow, which suits a day of looking rather than hurrying. Phonsavan, about nineteen kilometres away, has petrol stations, a few simple restaurants, and guesthouses that serve a hot breakfast of noodles. Try the local Lao coffee, which is grown on the nearby Bolaven plateau further south and tends to be strong and sweet. Evenings can be cold, particularly from December to February.

The best way to appreciate the jars is to see the major sites first, then use the smaller ones to understand how widely the culture spread. The big question, who made them and why, stays open, and the quiet hilltops are the right place to ponder it.
t.site 1@19.4,103.2:
If you only visit one cluster of jars, make it Site 1, which is the closest to Phonsavan and the largest, with more than three hundred stone vessels scattered across a broad grassy hill. Locals call it Thong Hai Hin. The biggest jar here is the star, a hulking block of sandstone taller than a man and said to weigh several tonnes, and it leans against a shoulder of the hill with a gentle air of fatigue. Around it, jars of all sizes lie in clusters, some standing, some fallen, some split along natural fractures. A few have rounded holes in their sides, perhaps from old damage or shelling.

Down the slope from the main field is a limestone cave with a large opening in its roof. Some think it served as a crematorium where bodies were burnt before the remains went into jars, and the smoke would have escaped through the hole. The cave is cool and echoing, and the story fits neatly with the funeral theory, though it is not proven. During the war, local people sheltered here from air raids, and the bomb craters pocking the hillside are a record of how heavy the bombing was. Many have filled with grass and wildflowers. The clear paths are marked with red and white stones, and the rule is simple: stay on the white side.

The ride from Phonsavan takes only about ten minutes on a flat paved road, through a landscape of rolling grass, small fields and little villages. It is an easy, relaxed journey, ideal for the morning. Traffic is mostly motorbikes, trucks and the odd tourist minibus. Fuel stations are along the main road in town, and Phonsavan has plenty of places to eat, mostly noodle shops and simple cafes.

The best light is early, when mist hangs in the hollows and the stones are dark with dew, or in the hour before sunset, when the sandstone turns amber. Crowds, such as they are, peak late morning. The plateau is cool, so bring a light layer in winter. The jars were added to the UNESCO list in 2019, together with several other sites, and they have earned it, because nowhere else in the world has anything quite like them.
t.site 3 group 7@19.3,103.1:
Group 7 is among the farthest-flung parts of Site 3, and its pleasure lies in solitude. The path leads over the shoulder of a hill and down through scrubby grass, past a small stand of trees, until a handful of jars comes into view. They are fewer than in the main groups, but each one sits alone in its own space, giving you a clear look at the carving. The stone is a pale, pinkish sandstone with a rough, pitted surface, and it takes on a rosy tint in the evening. Some jars have fallen over and lie like dropped hats, mouths turned toward the sky or the soil.

What makes the landscape easy to love is how modest it is. This is not a dramatic mountain scene. It is a soft, open upland with long grass, a few trees and the odd water buffalo, and the jars seem to have grown out of it. In the dry season the grass goes golden and the hills look like velvet, and in the wet it is bright green with mud on the tracks. Butterflies and small birds are everywhere, and the air smells of hay and woodsmoke from nearby farms.

A word on caution that no one should skip. Cluster munitions fell heavily on this area in the 1960s and early 1970s, and clearance teams are still at work. Paths at Site 3 are cleared and marked, and it is only safe to walk where the markers show. If the path is not clear, turn around. Children who live nearby know the land very well and sometimes act as unofficial guides, but it is better to arrive with a local guide arranged in Phonsavan.

Phonsavan, around eighteen kilometres off, is the base for everything, with fuel, food and simple places to sleep. The road from the town to Site 3 passes through villages where weavers sell cloth at stalls, and the surface is good until the last stretch, which can be rough in the wet season. Carry water and sun protection. From November to February the days are cool and clear, with sharp light on the stone.
t.site 3 group 2@19.3,103.1:
Group 2 gives you the sense of how the jars sit within working farmland. The cluster lies near a village, with fields running right up to the edge of the cleared path, and as you walk you pass rice stubble, a small irrigation channel and perhaps a woman carrying a load of firewood. The jars here are of medium size, some pushed over, some partly buried, and they are mixed with outcrops of natural rock. It all looks quite casual, as if the landscape had not noticed it was famous.

The Plain of Jars is a plateau in the north of Laos, built of sandstone and limestone, with the old kingdom of Xieng Khouang at its heart. For centuries the region was the home of the Phuan people, who ruled from Muang Khoun and traded with both Vietnam and Siam. Powerful neighbours sacked the town more than once. In the twentieth century, the plateau lay along the supply routes of the Vietnam War, and much of the old capital was destroyed in the bombing campaign. The people who farm the fields today have lived through all of this, and many of them work in clearing teams or run small guesthouses.

For riders, the plateau offers good, quiet roads. Route 7 and Route 6 cross the high country in long, easy bends with views of pine and grass, and in the cool season there is a bite in the air. From Phonsavan the road to the sites is paved for most of the way, though the last part can be bumpy. The days are warm and the evenings can be chilly, with mist in the valleys at dawn. In the dry months, from November to April, traffic is light. During the rains, mud and slippery surfaces call for caution.

You will find fuel in Phonsavan, and a modest range of food, from noodle soup to grilled meat and sticky rice. The local rice whisky, lao-lao, is strong and often offered with a smile, so go gently if you have a bike to ride. Plan a slow day, with time to look at the stones and to sit under a tree and think about the people who made them.
t.sine ngayene@13.7,-15.5:
Sine Ngayene is the largest of the stone circle sites in the Senegambian region, and it lies just across the border from Farafenni, on the Senegalese side. Here, in a field of grass and scattered trees, are dozens of circles made of tall, rust-brown pillars, each cut from laterite, a hard red rock found in the area. The sites of Sine Ngayene, Wassu, Kerbatch and Wanar together form the Senegambian Stone Circles, listed by UNESCO in 2006. The stones stand about two metres high, and some are cut in a distinctive shape, like a lyre, with a notch at the top. The group at Sine Ngayene has more than a thousand stones.

The circles are burial monuments. Excavations found graves beside and beneath the stones, with iron tools, pottery and beads, and the monuments are dated to somewhere between the third century BC and the sixteenth century AD. Nobody knows who built them, though the culture was clearly one of skilled ironworkers and farmers. The oral traditions of the Wolof and Mandinka peoples do not preserve any memory of the builders, which makes them all the more mysterious.

The approach is on the main road along the Gambia River, part of the Trans-Gambia Highway, which runs east to west through the Gambia and Senegal. At Farafenni, a long-standing ferry crossing was replaced in 2019 by the Senegambia Bridge, an important link, and the traffic of lorries has changed accordingly. The road surface has improved in recent years but can still have potholes and loose gravel on shoulders. Roadside police and army checkpoints are common, and politeness and patience go a long way. Goats, donkeys and children are often on the road.

Farafenni, about sixteen kilometres away, is a busy market town with fuel and basic food, andit draws people from across the region on market days. Sara Kunda, a smaller village, is further on. Eat what the locals eat, domoda, a groundnut stew, and benachin, a one-pot rice dish, and carry plenty of water. The hot season, from March to June, is intense. The best time to go is November to February, when the air is dry and mornings are cool.
t.ensemble mixte de fatu iva@-10.5,-138.7:
Fatu Hiva is the most remote of the inhabited Marquesas, the southernmost island of this far-flung French Polynesian group, and it feels it. Steep green mountains rise straight from the sea, and the two villages, Omoa in the south and Hanavave on the north-west coast, sit in valleys so tightly folded that you can look up from the beach and see rock walls running to the clouds. Hanavave's bay was originally called the Bay of Penises by French sailors for its rock spires, then prudishly changed to the Bay of Virgins.

For riders, this is a place for a very short and very serious road. A mountain route connects the two villages, climbing through the island's interior with sharp hairpins, steep grades and occasional damp, slippery patches, and the views, when the cloud lifts, show rainforest ridges tumbling into the Pacific. It is an adventure rather than a relaxed cruise, and in the wet season, which brings heavy downpours, it can be treacherous. There is no real touring network, and there are few vehicles on the island at all. Reaching Fatu Hiva usually requires the supply boat or a charter from Hiva Oa, and sea conditions affect schedules.

The island's culture is strongly alive. Fatu Hiva is known across the Pacific for its tapa, or bark cloth, beaten from the inner bark of the mulberry and breadfruit trees and decorated with traditional Marquesan designs, and for wood carving. The Norwegian explorer Thor Heyerdahl lived here in 1937 and 1938 with his wife, and his experience later fed into his theories about Polynesian origins, a story that is told with some mixed feelings by locals. Food is simple and good: fresh fish, breadfruit, coconut, and pamplemousse, the sweet giant grapefruit of the Marquesas, which is gloriously juicy.

On practical matters, services are minimal. The villages are small, with a few shops, small guesthouses, and almost no formal fuel supply, so do not plan on petrol except what you bring or can arrange with the locals. Bring cash in Pacific francs, insect repellent, a rain jacket, and patience. Ask permission before photographing people or sacred sites, since many are on family land, and remember that the schedule here is set by the sea and the weather.
t.funchal@32.7,-16.9:
Funchal climbs the sides of a natural amphitheatre on the south coast of Madeira, and from the harbour the houses rise in tiers into the green mountains behind. It is the island's capital, with about a hundred thousand people, and the name comes from funcho, the Portuguese word for fennel, which grew wild here when the first settlers arrived in the fifteenth century. Sugar made the island rich, then wine, and the legacy of both still shows in the tall merchant houses and the church interiors covered in gilded wood.

Madeira wine is the thing to try, a fortified wine heated during ageing, which gives it a caramel richness and a remarkable ability to last for decades. The old lodges in the town offer tastings. The Mercado dos Lavradores, the farmers' market, sells tropical fruit, flowers and fish, including the black scabbardfish, espada, which is a local favourite and is often served with banana. Poncha, a drink of rum, honey and lemon, is the local welcome. The toboggan runs, where men in straw hats guide wicker sledges down the hill from Monte, have been a tourist attraction since the nineteenth century.

The ride out is spectacular and demanding. The island is a mass of steep volcanic mountains, and the roads cling to the slopes, with sharp bends, short tunnels and sudden drops. The ER101 along the north coast passes waterfalls, laurel forest and cliffs, and the high roads near Pico do Arieiro, at around 1,800 metres, run above the clouds. The surface is generally good but can be slippery when wet, and fog and rain arrive suddenly, particularly in the mountains. Traffic in Funchal is dense, with steep streets and tight junctions, so the early miles need care.

Fuel and services are all here. Funchal has many stations, and others lie in villages around the island, but the north and west are quiet and stations are fewer, so fill up before heading out. The temperature is mild all year, with warm summers and little frost except at the highest points, and the best months are spring and autumn.

On your return, the lights of the city climbing the slopes make a fine sight. Look for a table with a view and order something grilled.
t.vientiane@18.0,102.6:
Vientiane is the quietest capital you are likely to meet, a low, tree-lined city on the northern bank of the Mekong where the river forms the border with Thailand. About two hundred thousand people live in the city proper, and the pace is so gentle that visitors often forget it is a capital at all. Monks in saffron robes walk the early streets, and in the evening the riverbank fills with people jogging, eating and watching the sunset over Thailand.

The city's symbols are religious and national. That Luang, a great golden stupa, stands on a broad plaza and is the emblem of Laos, with the current structure dating from the sixteenth century and rebuilt after damage. Patuxai, an arch inspired by the Arc de Triomphe but decorated with Lao motifs, was built in the 1960s from cement donated for an airport, which led to its nickname the vertical runway. Wat Si Saket, from the early nineteenth century, is among the oldest surviving temples in the city, with thousands of tiny Buddha images in niches along its cloister walls.

Outside the city, Buddha Park, about twenty-five kilometres east, is an odd and charming collection of concrete sculptures of Hindu and Buddhist deities, built in the 1950s by a mystic-sculptor. The Friendship Bridge, opened in 1994, links Laos to Thailand's Nong Khai, and a ride over it connects to the Thai roads toward Udon Thani. Roads around Vientiane are flat and broad, with scooters everywhere, though drivers are courteous by regional standards.

The heat and humidity are heavy, especially from March to May, and the rains fall from May to October, so the cool, dry months from November to February are the best. Petrol is easy to find, and so is food: sticky rice, laap, grilled river fish, and French bread with coffee. Beerlao is the national drink. Evening is the best time to be by the river, when the stalls light up and the heat finally lets go. Nothing here hurries, and it is easy to follow suit.
t.phu phrabat@17.7,102.4:
Imagine a forest of sandstone mushrooms, boulders balanced on pillars and arches sculpted by wind and rain, and you are close to the setting of Phu Phra Bat. The place lies on a low plateau in Udon Thani province, in north-east Thailand's Isan region, about eighteen kilometres from the town of Nam Som. Over millions of years, erosion has carved the rock into strange shapes, and people have used the overhangs and caves for shelter and worship since prehistoric times.

The name means Mountain of the Buddha's Footprint, and it refers to a hollow in the rock venerated as a footprint of the Buddha. The legend most visitors hear concerns the princess Usa and the prince Barot, a love story in which the princess's father, a ruler, set impossible tasks to separate them. Several rock formations carry their names, including a tower said to be her home, and the whole park feels like the stage set for a fairy tale.

History runs deep. Rock shelters are decorated with prehistoric paintings of hands and animals, while later peoples, in the first millennium AD, carved sema, boundary stones that mark sacred precincts, and set them around natural rock shrines. Statues of the Buddha were carved or placed in natural niches. In 2024 UNESCO inscribed the park as a World Heritage site, recognising it as part of the sema stone tradition of the Dvaravati culture.

The ride across Isan is flat to gently rolling, with rice fields, sugar cane, eucalyptus and small villages. Roads are good and quiet, with long straight sections, though trucks and motorbikes carry loads of every kind. Heat is intense from March to May, and the rains from June to October turn the fields green and the dirt tracks to mud. Cool dry weather from November to February is best. The park has a modest entry fee, paths and signs, and a small cafe; fuel is easy in Nam Som and Ban Phue, where you can also buy sticky rice and grilled chicken for lunch.
t.the phu phrabat historical park@17.7,102:
The park of Phu Phra Bat holds more than its rocks, and what lies between them tells the story. Among the sandstone outcrops of this north-east Thai plateau, hundreds of stones have been set upright in the ground, flat slabs shaped like leaves, which are the sema that mark the boundary of a sacred space. This practice is typical of the Dvaravati period, between about the seventh and eleventh centuries, when Buddhism flourished in the region before the Khmer empire extended its power.

The sema are often carved with scenes from the Buddha's previous lives, the Jataka tales, in a style distinct from that of other regions. Around them the monks and lay people shaped caves into shrines, placed images of the Buddha under natural rock roofs, and carved steps to reach the best viewpoints. Later, the Lao and Khmer cultures left their own marks. The result is a landscape in which nature and devotion cannot be separated.

For a visitor, the walk is the point. Sandy paths wind between boulders, past caves like Tham Wua and Tham Khon, where fig roots grip the stone, and the forest is dry deciduous woodland of dipterocarps that turns green in the rainy season and dusty gold in the dry. Birdsong in the early morning is lovely, and so are the geckos in the caves. The ground can be slippery after rain, so wear shoes, and carry water, because the shade is patchy and the sun strong.

From a motorbike's point of view, the roads in this region are easy and quiet, with the odd stray dog and slow tractor. Fuel stations are frequent on the main highways, and Nam Som, Ban Phue and Udon Thani have a good choice of restaurants, with grilled fish, papaya salad and sticky rice as the staples. Weekdays are quiet, with Thai pilgrims arriving on holidays and festivals. A dawn visit gives you the best light and the cooler air.
t.kunta kinteh island and related sites@13:
In the brown tidal water of the River Gambia, some thirty kilometres from the Atlantic, a small low island of rock and scrub carries the ruins of a fort that mattered far beyond its size. For centuries Portuguese, Courlanders, English and French all fought to control this reach of the river, the gateway to the gold, ivory, wax and, above all, people that came down from the interior. The island was long called James Island, after a Stuart prince, and in 2011 its name was officially changed to Kunta Kinteh, after the ancestor in Alex Haley's novel Roots, who is said to have been taken from the nearby village of Juffureh. Whether or not the family story holds in every detail, the island stands for the whole trade, and the World Heritage listing covers the island and its related sites on the banks.

You reach it by boat from Albreda, in a few minutes across muddy water with pelicans and egrets on the mangrove edge. What remains is a broken wall, a few cannon and a bit of the old warehouse, and the baobab on the island is a landmark visible for miles. The ruin is slowly being eaten by the river, and the fragility is part of its power. A small museum in Albreda tells the story, and local guides explain it with a calm that comes from long practice.

The ride to the north bank starts at Banjul, where you take the ferry across the river mouth to Barra, which can involve a long wait, since the crossing is slow and crowded, and then continues east on the main road toward Albreda and Juffureh. The tarmac is generally decent but patched, and the heat, dust, goats, donkeys and people walking on the shoulder call for a slow pace. From November to March the weather is dry and bearable, and the rains from June to October turn some tracks to mud.

Fuel is best taken at Barra or Essau before heading on, because the villages near the river may have none, and cash is essential. The nearest listed town, Lamin, is about nine kilometres from the island, and Essau is further north. Bring water, and watch for the fishing boats pulled up on the shore in the evening.
t.maurel freres building@13.3,-16.4:
The Maurel Frères building at Albreda is a plain, solid trading house of the kind that once lined the West African coast, and it tells the commercial side of the Gambia story. Albreda was a French trading post from the late seventeenth century, wedged into a river that the British otherwise controlled, and for roughly a hundred and fifty years the French and British argued about it. France finally gave up its claim to the little enclave in 1857, but the French firms stayed. Maurel Frères, a trading house from Bordeaux, had a presence along this coast, and its warehouse here, built of brick and stone with a pitched roof, handled the trade that replaced the slave trade: groundnuts, beeswax, hides and rubber.

The groundnut, or peanut, deserves a mention, since it shaped the country. In the nineteenth century farmers along the river were persuaded to grow it for export, and for generations it was the Gambia's main crop, bought by traders, shipped to Europe and pressed for oil. The building stands as a reminder that the shift from one trade to another left the same riverbank economy in place, with merchants and middlemen, a landing and a warehouse, and the farmers at the bottom of the chain. Next to it is the old landing stage, from which boats still cross to the island.

Albreda is a quiet village with sandy lanes, mango trees and a small market, and the old buildings are in various states of repair, some restored and some crumbling under creepers. A local guide will take you around for a modest fee, and the museum nearby is worth a stop. The riverside has a laid-back feel, with fishermen mending nets and children playing on the sand.

The road to the village from the Barra ferry is a long and flat route through farmland, palms and bush, with a mix of tarmac and potholed patches, and the hazards are those of any West African road, with goats, minibuses and people on foot. Ride in daylight and take it slowly. Fuel can be bought at Barra or Essau, and nothing should be assumed in the villages. The dry months from November to February are kindest, with warm days and cool nights, and the light on the river in the early morning is pale gold.
t.ruins of san domingo@13.3,-16.4:
Before the French and the British came to this stretch of the Gambia, the Portuguese were here, and the ruins of San Domingo are what is left of their presence. Portuguese traders and settlers moved up the river in the sixteenth century, married into local families and built a small community with a chapel, a handful of houses and storehouses on the north bank near Juffureh. They traded cloth, iron and beads for wax, hides, ivory and slaves, and their descendants, often of mixed ancestry, became middlemen for later European traders. What survives is a fragment of wall, the outline of a chapel or church and some brick foundations in a patch of ground under baobab and mango trees.

It is a small and modest site, which is exactly why it is moving. Nothing about the ruin shouts, and its brick walls are being reclaimed by roots and termites, but it marks the beginning of a story that ran for three centuries. The broader ensemble listed by UNESCO includes the island, the fort remains and the villages of Albreda and Juffureh, and this ruin gives the earliest layer. Juffureh, a short walk away, is the village linked in Alex Haley's Roots to the ancestor Kunta Kinteh, and it has a small museum and a market where women sell batik cloth and carved wooden masks. Fuel is available at Barra and Essau, and the nearest bigger town on the map is Lamin, about six kilometres away, but supplies in small villages are unreliable, so fill up and carry water. The dry season from November to April is the comfortable time.

It has been partly restored as part of the heritage area, and its tall doors and shuttered windows give a sense of the heat and routine of the old trading day. Boats leave from the landing for the island, and local guides explain the history with the aid of a small museum, where displays include the chains and trade goods that tell the harsher side of the story.
