t.nan@18.8,100.8:
Nan is a small, calm provincial capital in a mountain-ringed valley in the far north of Thailand, close to the Laos border, and it has stayed quieter than Chiang Mai or Chiang Rai. The Nan river runs through the plain, and the old kingdom here was a separate Lanna state with its own princes until the early twentieth century. The temples keep the northern style, with steep roofs, carved gables and gilded flourishes, and the town has the unhurried air of a place that visitors are only beginning to find.

The best-known building is Wat Phumin, a sixteenth-century temple shaped like a cross, with four doorways opening to four Buddha figures seated back to back around a central pillar. Inside, the walls are covered with murals from the nineteenth century showing daily life in the Lanna period, including a pair of lovers, one whispering to the other, that has become the town's emblem. Not far away, Wat Phra That Chae Haeng, on a hill outside town, has a golden spire that is said to contain a relic of the Buddha and is the centre of the area's religious life. Each autumn, boat races are held on the river, with long, ornate dragon-headed craft.

For a rider, Nan is a real treat because the roads leaving it are some of the most enjoyable in northern Thailand. Highway 1081 runs north into the mountains toward Bo Kluea, climbing through forest and over ridges, with long sweeping bends, good surface and little traffic, then crosses into the Doi Phu Kha National Park, where the hills are covered with cloud forest and the wild Chaloem Phra Kiat cherry trees blossom in winter. At Bo Kluea, an old well pumps salt from underground brine, and local families still boil it down in the traditional way. Traffic drives on the left, and the occasional dog or buffalo on the road deserves respect.

The hot season from March to May brings smoke from agricultural burning, which can make the air hazy and unpleasant, and the rains from June to October make the roads slippery. The cool months of November to February are the best for riding, with clear skies and fresh mornings.

Nan has fuel stations and cafes on every main road, and the night market is a good place for local dishes such as khao soi and sticky rice with grilled pork. Fill up before heading into the hills, as the stations thin out beyond the villages.
t.the sima cultural site at wat phra phuth:
A sima is a boundary stone, and in the north-east of Thailand, in the region called Isan, hundreds of them stand in fields and temple grounds, many of them more than a thousand years old. Monks placed them in rings around ordination halls, to mark the sacred space where the Buddhist community could meet, and in the Dvaravati period, between roughly the seventh and eleventh centuries, carvers began to decorate them with scenes from the life of the Buddha. The sima at the site in this listing are part of a UNESCO inscription that recognises this tradition, found nowhere else in such density.

The stones are often slabs of the local sandstone, standing upright and weathered by rain, with reliefs showing the Buddha's birth, his teaching and scenes from his earlier lives, drawn in a simple, vigorous style. Sometimes they are placed in the shelter of rock formations, among boulders, and sometimes in an open temple compound under tall trees. The whole region is dotted with sandstone outcrops and rock shelters, some with prehistoric paintings, which made it a place of religious significance long before the Dvaravati period.

The ride from Vientiane begins across the Mekong by the Friendship Bridge, which Thai and Lao authorities have operated since 1994, with border formalities to deal with on both sides, then continues through Nong Khai and south along the highway to Udon Thani. The road is straight, flat and fast, with long views of rice fields, sugar cane and cassava, and the main hazard is slow trucks. Thailand drives on the left, so riders from Laos have to switch sides at the crossing. The best months are November to February, when it is cool and dry. From April to October, heat and heavy rain make it harder.

Nam Som, the nearest sizeable town, has about nineteen thousand people and is a good place to buy fuel, food and water. Thai roadside restaurants are excellent: look for grilled chicken, papaya salad, sticky rice and sweet iced tea, the staples of Isan cooking. Bring cash, and remember to take off your shoes before entering temple buildings. Go early, since the sun is hot, and the stones are best seen in low light.
t.xining@36.6,101.8:
Xining stands on the edge of the Tibetan Plateau, at about 2,200 metres, and it is the capital of Qinghai Province, a city of more than seven hundred thousand people in a valley between high, dry hills. It is a meeting point of cultures: Han Chinese, Tibetan, Hui Muslim and Mongol communities all live here, and you can see it in the street food, the mosques and the monasteries. The Dongguan Great Mosque, one of the largest in northwest China, stands near the old centre, and the smell of grilled lamb and baking bread drifts from the Muslim quarter.

Twenty-five kilometres from the city lies the Ta'er Monastery, or Kumbum, one of the six great monasteries of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, founded in the sixteenth century at the birthplace of Tsongkhapa, the school's founder. It is a large complex of temples and prayer halls, with famous butter sculptures and a steady flow of pilgrims. It is well worth a visit for anyone who wants to understand the region, and it is a good warm-up for the altitude.

For riders, Xining is the beginning of a very serious road. The Qinghai-Tibet Highway, the G109, runs southwest across the plateau toward Golmud and eventually Lhasa, crossing passes of over 4,700 metres, and further on over 5,000 metres, with thin air, strong wind and sudden snow. Qinghai Lake, the largest in China, lies to the west and is a good first target, with a ride along its shore through rapeseed fields in July. The road is mostly paved, and the main dangers are altitude, cold and heavy trucks.

For foreign visitors, riding here is far from simple, because rules on vehicles, licences and permits are strict and change often, so check the current regulations well in advance. Fuel is plentiful in the city, and you should fill up whenever possible once on the highway, since the distances between stations grow. Take time to acclimatise, drink water and listen to your body, because altitude sickness can strike anyone. The sky is huge, the light is hard and bright, and the road ahead is one of the great journeys in Asia.
t.ribeira brava@32.7,-17.1:
Ribeira Brava is a south-coast Madeira town that sits at the mouth of a deep valley and the foot of the old road across the island. A small bay of dark pebbles, a church with a handsome tiled tower, a seafront that locals actually use, and then the mountains rise straight behind. It has roughly six thousand people, so petrol, cash machines, bakeries and a decent lunch are all easy, which is exactly what a start point should offer.

Madeira's coast is steep volcanic rock cut by ravines, and this valley is one of the big ones. The old road climbs from sea level to the Encumeada Pass at about a thousand metres in a tight sequence of hairpins and shaded bends, past terraced banana plots, vines, and the little stone levada channels that carry water around the hillsides. The expressway tunnels have taken most of the traffic, which is a gift: the old route is quiet, narrow in places, occasionally scattered with rockfall after rain, and a wonderful bike road if you like riding up a mountain with the view slowly widening behind you.

The history is mostly sugar and wine. In the sixteenth century this coast made a fortune from sugar cane, and later the island's fortified wine became famous around the Atlantic world. Even now you will see cane being grown and the local honey-cane rum served in the bars. The island rises from the ocean without a shelf, so weather behaves strangely: you can leave in bright sun at the shore and meet cloud and drizzle on the plateau above, then drop out of it again on the far side. Pack a thin waterproof whatever the forecast says.

Past Encumeada the ride opens onto the Paul da Serra, a high moorland plateau at about fourteen hundred metres, treeless and windy, with grazing cattle and a long straight road that feels like another country. Fuel is not available up there, so fill in Ribeira Brava or nearby Ponta do Sol before you start. Try a bolo do caco, the flat bread cooked on a stone, hot with garlic butter, and a poncha, the local lemon and spirit mix, but save that second one until the bike is parked for the day.
t.kong lor@18.0,104.8:
Kong Lor is a river that goes through a mountain. The Hinboun river, swollen by monsoon rains, flows into a vast cave entrance at the foot of a limestone ridge, and travels underground for about seven kilometres before emerging on the other side, in a green valley with rice paddies and buffalo. Visitors go through it in a long, narrow wooden boat, with a boatman at the stern and a guide with a headlamp at the bow, and the experience is a mixture of the ridiculous and the sublime: a tiny light in a gigantic dark space, with stalactites, echoing chambers and the soft slap of the water.

The cave is in the Phou Hin Poun protected area, a region of dramatic limestone karst in Khammouane province, and the village of Kong Lor is the usual gateway. A short walk through the entrance hall leads to the boat landing, and the journey takes a little over an hour each way, with a stop midway where visitors can step out to see formations lit by torches. In the dry season, the water is low and passengers sometimes walk past rapids. The area has become one of Laos's best-loved attractions, and so it can be busy in the middle of the day.

The road to the cave is a highlight of the Thakhek Loop. It winds through karst valleys with rice fields and small villages, with towers of limestone looming over the road. The tarmac is mostly good, but in places it breaks down into potholes or has loose gravel, particularly after rain, and the corners can come quickly. Animals are common on the road. Mornings are the best time for riding, when the air is cooler and the light is soft on the rock, and the mist is rising from the valleys.

There is little in the way of services at Kong Lor beyond guesthouses, simple restaurants and a few shops, so organise fuel and cash in advance, using the larger towns on the loop. Small stalls sell fuel in bottles, but you will not want to depend on them. Evenings are quiet, with the sound of frogs and the glow of lamps, and a river view from a hammock is the ideal way to end the day. Bring a torch of your own, and wear shoes you do not mind getting wet.
t.thakhek loop point 4@18.0,104.8:
Konglor Cave is one of the great natural wonders of Southeast Asia, a limestone tunnel about seven kilometres long through which the Nam Hin Bun river flows from one side of a mountain to the other. Visitors travel through it by long wooden boats, powered by small outboard motors and steered by local guides, sitting in near darkness with only headlamps to light the way. The cavern is vast, with ceilings that disappear into blackness, and in places formations of stalactites are lit up in colour. Midway, you stop and walk through a chamber filled with towering shapes of rock.

The road to the cave leaves the main highway and runs for about forty kilometres through farmland and forest, with the limestone peaks rising on both sides. The surface is mostly sealed, though it narrows and has potholes, especially in the wet season, and village life spills out on to the road with children, chickens and buffalo. Corners are gentle, with the occasional sharp bend, and the views of cliffs at the end of fields are fantastic. In the dry season the dust can be thick behind trucks.

The valley around the cave is home to villages of Lao and minority peoples, who farm rice and tobacco and fish in the river. A handful of guesthouses and homestays near the cave offer food and a bed, and boat tickets are bought at the entrance. The river through the cave can run high after heavy rain, and boats do not operate in floods, so allow flexibility.

Fuel is not available near the cave, so fill up in Ban Na Hin before coming here, and carry spare if your bike has a small tank. Bring a torch or headlamp, a waterproof bag for your phone and a change of dry clothes if you plan to walk. The cooler months, from November to February, are the best time to visit. Sunsets over the fields are magnificent.
